q.s:
In a certain city, the population mean commute time to work was reported as 30 minutes. The director of human resources for a certain company in the city claimed the mean commute time for the company’s employees was greater than 30 minutes. The director surveyed 35 randomly selected employees and found that their mean commute time was 31.4 minutes. With all conditions for inference met, a hypothesis test conducted at the significance level α=0.05 resulted in a p-value of 0.381.

Which of the following is an appropriate conclusion?

o.l: The director has convincing statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean commute time is greater than 30 minutes.
The director has convincing statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean commute time is less than 30 minutes.
The director has convincing statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean commute time is 31.4 minutes.
The director does not have convincing statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean commute time is greater than 30 minutes.
The director does not have convincing statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean commute time is less than 30 minutes.

q.ex: In hypothesis testing, we compare the p-value to the significance level α to make a decision. The null hypothesis is that the population mean commute time equals 30 minutes, while the alternative hypothesis is that it is greater than 30 minutes (since the director claimed it was greater). The p-value of 0.381 is much larger than α = 0.05, which means we fail to reject the null hypothesis. When we fail to reject the null hypothesis, we do not have sufficient evidence to support the alternative hypothesis. Therefore, the director does not have convincing statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean commute time is greater than 30 minutes.

q.s: Most dermatologists recommend that the ideal shower lasts approximately 10 minutes. A researcher suspects that the average shower length of high school students is greater than 10 minutes. To test the belief, the researcher surveyed 125 randomly selected high school students and found that their average shower length was 14.7 minutes. With all conditions for inference met, a hypothesis test was conducted at the significance level of α=0.05, and the test produced a p-value of 0.0000. Which of the following is an appropriate conclusion?

o.l: The test was flawed because the p-value cannot equal 0.
The researcher has statistical evidence to conclude that the sample mean shower length for high school students is greater than 10 minutes.
The researcher does not have statistical evidence to conclude that the sample mean shower length for high school students is greater than 10 minutes.
The researcher has statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean shower length for high school students is greater than 10 minutes.
The researcher does not have statistical evidence to conclude that the population mean shower length for high school students is greater than 10 minutes.

q.s:
A sociologist studying the difference in ages between husbands and wives obtained a random sample of 55 married couples. The mean of the husbands’ ages was 38.5 years with standard deviation 12.6 years. The mean of the wives’ ages was 36.9 years with standard deviation 12.4 years. The sociologist calculated the difference between the ages for each couple. The mean difference was 1.6 years with standard deviation 2.1 years. A matched-pairs hypothesis test will be performed to investigate whether the difference is significant.

Which of the following is the standard error for the test statistic for the hypothesis test?

o.l: 12.6255+12.4255
2.155
2.155+55
12.6−12.455
12.6−12.455+55

q.ex:
For a matched-pairs hypothesis test, we analyze the differences within each pair rather than comparing two independent samples. The key information is that the differences between husband and wife ages have a mean of 1.6 years and a standard deviation of 2.1 years across the 55 couples.

The standard error for a matched-pairs test is calculated as the standard deviation of the differences divided by the square root of the sample size: SE = s_d / sqrt(n), where s_d is the standard deviation of the differences and n is the number of pairs.

Substituting the given values: SE = 2.1 / sqrt(55).

If the mean typing speed of workers from the agency is less than 60 wpm, the probability of selecting a sample of 50 workers with mean 58.8 wpm or less is 0.267.

A manufacturer is experimenting with a new culture that claims to produce a pH of 5.2, which is perfect for cheddar cheese. A set of 50 test batches resulted in an average pH of 5.11. A one-sample t-test was conducted to investigate whether there is evidence that the mean pH is different from 5.2. The test resulted in a p-value of 0.018.

A fast-food restaurant claims that a small order of french fries contains 120 calories. A nutritionist is concerned that the true average calorie count is higher than that. The nutritionist randomly selects 35 small orders of french fries and determines their calories. The resulting sample mean is 155.6 calories, and the p-value for the hypothesis test is 0.00093.

Which of the following is the appropriate test for the researcher’s hypothesis?

o.l: A matched-pairs t-test for a mean difference
A two-sample t-test for a difference between means
A one-sample z-test for a population mean

Since the researcher is testing a hypothesis about the population mean length of salmon, not a proportion, a test for proportion is inappropriate. The choice between a z-test and t-test depends on whether the population standard deviation is known. q.s:
A forester reported the following distribution of tree types to a local logging company.

Tree Type Spruce Pine Fir Deciduous Other
Percent 52% 22% 8% 10% 8%

The logging company generated a random sample of 100 trees and observed the following distribution of trees in each of the categories.

Tree Type Spruce Pine Fir Deciduous Other
Observed Count 51 21 10 9 9

The logging company would like to use its sample to provide convincing statistical evidence that over 50 percent of the trees in the forest are spruce trees. The logging company has decided to use a chi-square goodness-of-fit test to justify its claim. Why is the chi-square goodness-of-fit test not an appropriate procedure for the logging company to use?

o.l: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test would be used to show that the entire distribution of trees in the forest is different than what the forester reported, not necessarily the individual proportion representing the spruce trees.

The logging company should find the average number of spruce trees using several samples and then construct a confidence interval for a difference in population means to show that there are more spruce trees in the forest than reported.
The logging company does not need to complete an inference procedure; there are more than 50 percent spruce trees in the sample.

In order to perform a chi-square test, the logging company needs expected counts, not percentages. The logging company should declare its current sample as expected values and then generate a new sample of observed values to compute the test statistic.
The sample does not meet the minimum requirements needed for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.

The logging company wants to test specifically whether the proportion of spruce trees exceeds 0.50, which is a hypothesis about one proportion, not about the overall distribution. Which of the following is an appropriate test for the investigation?

o.l: A one-sample t-test for a population mean
A one-sample t-test for a sample mean
A one-sample z-test for a population proportion
A two-sample t-test for a difference between population means
A matched-pairs t-test for a mean difference

Topic:7.4: Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean
q.ex: The analyst is testing whether the population mean purchase amount exceeds $100 using data from one sample. Since the population standard deviation is unknown and the sample standard deviation ($5.30) must be used instead, a t-test is required rather than a z-test. The sample size is 56, which is reasonably large but not large enough to invoke the Central Limit Theorem to justify using a z-test when the population parameter is unknown. Only one sample is being compared to a hypothesized value ($100), so this is a one-sample test. The test concerns the population mean, not the sample mean, because hypothesis tests always make inferences about population parameters

A one-sample z-test for a population proportion
A two-sample t-test for a difference between means

Since the executive is testing whether the current population mean differs from a known value (last year's mean), this requires a one-sample test for a population mean. The choice between z-test and t-test depends on whether the population standard deviation is known. Because the executive calculates the sample standard deviation (not the population standard deviation), a t-test is appropriate. A two-sample t-test would be incorrect because there is only one sample being collected (this year's data), with last year's mean serving as the comparison value rather than requiring a second sample

q.ex: The p-value represents the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the observed value, not the probability of observing that exact value. Henry's interpretation incorrectly states that the p-value of 0.03 is the probability of observing χ² = 12.4 exactly. The correct interpretation is that 0.03 is the probability of observing χ² ≥ 12.4 (or a value at least as extreme), assuming the null hypothesis is true. This distinction is crucial because for continuous distributions like the chi-square distribution, the probability of any single exact value is essentially zero.

The researcher interpreted the p-value as the probability of observing 1.92 exactly.

A six-week fitness program was designed to decrease the time it takes retired individuals to walk one mile. At the beginning of the program, 20 randomly selected retired individuals were invited to participate, and their times to walk a mile were recorded. After the six-week program, their times to walk a mile were again recorded. Most participants saw little to no improvement in their times to walk one mile; however, a few participants saw drastic improvements in their times to walk one mile. The program director would like to perform a hypothesis test to determine if the program reduces the mean time for retired individuals to walk a mile.

Which of the following statements is true?

o.l: Because there are 40 observations in total, the sample size is large enough to assume that the sampling distribution of the sample mean differences is approximately normal.
Because the walk times before and after the program are paired, a hypothesis test is not appropriate.
The sampling distribution of sample means can be assumed to be approximately normal because the distribution of the sample data is not skewed.

Because the sample size of 20 is less than 30 and the improvements in walk times in the sample data appear to be skewed, the distribution of sample means should not be assumed to be approximately normal.
Because the program recruited only retired individuals, the distribution of sample means should not be assumed to be approximately normal.

q.ex: This is a paired data scenario where the same 20 individuals are measured before and after the program, so we analyze the differences in walk times for each person (not 40 independent observations). The key issue is whether we can assume the sampling distribution of mean differences is approximately normal. The Central Limit Theorem allows us to assume normality for the sampling distribution when the sample size is large (typically n ≥ 30) OR when the population distribution is approximately normal. Here, n = 20, which is less than 30, and the problem explicitly states that the distribution of improvements is skewed (most saw little improvement, but a few saw drastic improvements).

q.ex: The chi-square distribution is formed by summing squared standard normal random variables, which means all values must be non-negative with a lower bound at zero. As degrees of freedom increase, the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped, but with low degrees of freedom, the right skew is pronounced. The distribution is not approximately normal (which would have one central peak), nor is it skewed to the right (which would show a long tail extending rightward with one peak on the left). Bimodal

Skewed to the right
Symmetric and unimodal

f.c: The distributions of four variables are shown in the following histograms.

q.ex: To determine which shape is NOT represented, we need to identify the characteristics of the four distributions shown. A uniform distribution has approximately equal frequencies across all values, appearing as a flat or rectangular shape. A bimodal distribution has two distinct peaks. Skewed left distributions have a tail extending toward lower values with the peak on the right, while skewed right distributions have a tail extending toward higher values with the peak on the left. A symmetric and unimodal distribution has one central peak with balanced tails on both sides. Among the four distributions presented, there is no flat, rectangular pattern characteristic of a uniform distribution, making it the shape that is NOT represented.

q.s: Which of the following statements is a correct description of a feature of the study?

o.l: The study has replication because there are four types of exercise.
The study has replication because it was conducted over a six-week period.
The response variable is the type of exercise with the greatest change in maximal oxygen consumption.
The treatments in the study are strength training, flexibility training, aerobics, and jogging.
The experimental units are the four different types of exercise.

f.c: The director of a community recreation center conducted a six-week study to examine the effects of four types of exercise—strength training, flexibility training, aerobics, and jogging—on maximal oxygen consumption. From the 40 members who participated, the director randomly assigned 10 members to each exercise type. Maximal oxygen consumption was measured for each member at the beginning of the study and again at the end of the six weeks.

q.ex: In experimental design, treatments are the conditions deliberately imposed on experimental units by researchers. The four types of exercise—strength training, flexibility training, aerobics, and jogging—represent different conditions being tested, making them the treatments. Replication refers to applying treatments to multiple experimental units, not to having multiple treatment types or conducting a study over time. The response variable is what is measured (likely oxygen consumption changes), not which treatment performed best. Experimental units are the subjects receiving treatments (the participants), not the exercise types themselves. Option i4 correctly identifies the treatments as the four types of exercise being compared in the study.

q.s: Based on the design of the investigation, which of the following is the largest population to which the results can be generalized?

o.l: The 25 student athletes assigned to the beetroot juice group
The 50 student athletes in the sample
All student athletes at the college
All students at the college
All people who exercise

f.c: To investigate whether the consumption of beetroot juice enhances exercise performance, a researcher selected a random sample of 50 student athletes from all the student athletes at a college. The athletes in the sample were randomly assigned to one of two groups. In one group, 25 athletes were given a daily dose of beetroot juice, and in the other group, the remaining athletes were given a daily dose of a placebo. At the end of six weeks of exercise training, the researcher compared the performances of the two groups.

q.ex: The generalizability of results depends on how the sample was selected from the population. When a random sample is drawn from a specific population, results can be generalized to that entire population. Since the 50 student athletes were randomly selected from all student athletes at the college, the results can be generalized to all student athletes at the college. The results cannot be generalized beyond this group (to all students or all people who exercise) because those populations were not part of the sampling frame. The results also should not be limited to just the 50 participants in the sample, as proper random sampling allows inference to the broader population from which they were drawn. The graph shows the percent of surveys returned and not returned for each delivery method.

q.ex: To determine the appropriate test, we need to identify the data structure and research question. A matched-pairs t-test is used when comparing two measurements on the same subjects or when subjects are paired in a meaningful way, and we're interested in the mean of the differences. This differs from a two-sample t-test, which compares means from two independent groups. The matched-pairs design accounts for within-subject or within-pair correlation, making it more powerful when such pairing exists. Since the investigation involves paired observations rather than independent samples, proportions, or categorical relationships, the matched-pairs t-test is appropriate. The correct choice is a matched-pairs t-test

q.s: To compare the effectiveness of two treatments, researchers conducted a well-designed experiment using a randomized block design in which the subjects were blocked by age-group (under 40 years and 40 years or older). q.ex: In a randomized block design, subjects are first grouped into blocks based on a characteristic that might affect the response variable—in this case, age group. Within each block, treatments are then randomly assigned to subjects. This randomization within blocks is the defining feature that distinguishes a randomized block design from simply stratifying subjects. The purpose is to control for the blocking variable while still maintaining random assignment of treatments. Option i2 correctly describes this essential characteristic: treatments must be randomly assigned to subjects within each block. The distribution of sale price for a certain model of car is approximately normal with mean $22,500 and standard deviation $600.

Based on the distribution, which statement must be true?

o.l: Approximately 99% of the cars have a sale price less than $ 23 , 700 .
Approximately 84% of the cars have a sale price greater than $21,900.
Approximately 95% of the cars have a sale price between $21,900 and $23,100.
The interquartile range of the sale prices is approximately $600.
The minimum sale price is $20,700.

q.ex:
To solve this problem, we need to check each statement using the empirical rule and z-scores for a normal distribution with mean $22,500 and standard deviation $600.

For option i2: $21,900 is one standard deviation below the mean ($22,500 - $600 = $21,900). In a normal distribution, approximately 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, meaning 34% fall between the mean and one standard deviation below. Since 50% of values are above the mean, approximately 50% + 34% = 84% of cars have prices greater than $21,900.

A medical researcher is interested in assessing the effectiveness of a new medication for pain relief. Three hundred volunteers will be randomly assigned to groups. One group will receive the new medication at a low dose, one group will receive the new medication at a high dose, and one group will receive a placebo that looks like the new medication but does not contain any active ingredients. Each person will be asked to rate his or her level of pain at the beginning of the experiment and again two hours after taking the medication or placebo.

What is the number of treatments for this experiment?

o.l: 2
3
6
100
300

q.ex: In experimental design, a treatment is a specific condition or combination of conditions applied to experimental units. The number of treatments equals the number of distinct experimental conditions being compared, not the number of subjects or measurements. In this experiment, there are three distinct conditions: low-dose medication, high-dose medication, and placebo. The fact that pain is measured at two time points (beginning and two hours later) does not create additional treatments; these are simply repeated measurements of the response variable. The 300 volunteers represent the sample size, not the number of treatments. Therefore, the correct answer is 3 because there are exactly three different treatment conditions being administered to the three groups.

Which of the following is a correct interpretation of the interval?

We are 95% confident that the population mean weight of African bush elephants is between 12.2 thousand pounds and 14.6 thousand pounds.
We are 95% confident that the population mean weight of African bush elephants is 13.4 thousand pounds, which is the midpoint of the interval.
We are 95% confident that the mean weight calculated from a different sample of African bush elephants would be between 12.2 thousand pounds and 14.6 thousand pounds.

q.ex: A confidence interval for a population parameter provides a range of plausible values for that parameter based on sample data. The correct interpretation of a 95 percent confidence interval is that we are 95 percent confident the true population parameter (in this case, the population mean weight) falls within the interval. Option i1 is incorrect because it confuses the population mean with individual values—the interval estimates the mean, not the proportion of individual elephants. Option i2 is incorrect because once the interval is constructed, the population mean either is or is not in it; probability does not apply to a fixed parameter. Clark drives through two traffic lights on his way to work each day. From experience, he estimates that the probability that the first light will be red when he reaches it is 0.3. He also estimates that the probability that the second light will be red when he reaches it is 0.45. The lights are far enough apart that they can be considered to operate independently of each other.

Based on Clark’s estimates, what is the probability that at least one of the two lights will be red on a randomly selected drive to work?

o.l: 0.135

0.750

q.ex:
To find the probability that at least one light is red, use the complement rule: P(at least one red) = 1 - P(both green). 

The probability the first light is green is 1 - 0.3 = 0.7. The probability the second light is green is 1 - 0.45 = 0.55. Since the lights operate independently, the probability both are green is 0.7 × 0.55 = 0.385.

Therefore, P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.385 = 0.615.

Which of the following is a reasonable conclusion?

When the p-value exceeds the significance threshold, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, which in this case states there is no relationship between sleep and memory. This does not prove that no relationship exists; rather, it indicates the data do not provide sufficient evidence to conclude a relationship exists. Which of the following scatterplots most likely exhibits a violation of that condition?
q.ex: The condition being tested is constant variance (homoscedasticity), which requires that the spread of residuals around the regression line remains consistent across all values of the explanatory variable. A violation occurs when variability changes systematically as the explanatory variable increases or decreases, creating a pattern known as heteroscedasticity. According to the description, option i2 explicitly states that "as the value of the explanatory variable increases, the variability of the response variability increases," which is a classic fan-shaped or funnel pattern. Number of cookies sold 50 100 200
Probability 0.60 0.35 0.05

The probability distribution of the number of cookies sold by a store each day is shown in the table. The store earns a profit of $0.50 per cookie sold.

What is the store’s expected daily profit for the sales of the cookies?

o.l: $37.50
$75.00
$116.67
$150.00
$175.00

q.ex:
To find the expected daily profit, first calculate the expected number of cookies sold, then multiply by the profit per cookie.

The expected value formula is E(X) = Σ[x · P(x)], where x represents each outcome and P(x) its probability.

Expected cookies sold = (50)(0.60) + (100)(0.35) + (200)(0.05) = 30 + 35 + 10 = 75 cookies.

Since the store earns $0.50 profit per cookie, the expected daily profit = 75 cookies × $0.50/cookie = $37.

The design is randomized because the order in which students complete the two trials is randomized, controlling for potential order effects like fatigue or learning. This is not a completely randomized experiment because subjects are not randomly assigned to independent groups; instead, each subject receives both treatments. It is not observational because the researchers actively manipulate the treatment conditions rather than simply observing existing behaviors.

A medical researcher conducted a study to investigate the effectiveness of two drugs, L and M, designed to reduce the number of seizures that people with epilepsy might have. Each person in a group of 120 adult volunteers who had epilepsy was randomly assigned to one of two groups. Those assigned to one group took drug L for one year, and those assigned to the other group took drug M for one year. Each participant recorded the number of seizures that occurred during the year.

To which group is it most reasonable to generalize the results of this study?

o.l: All adults
All adults with epilepsy
All adults with epilepsy who take drugs to treat the disease
All adults with epilepsy who are similar to those who volunteered for the study
All adults who experience a reduction in the number of seizures

q.ex: The key to determining the appropriate population for generalization is identifying who the sample actually represents. The study used 120 adult volunteers with epilepsy, which is a self-selected sample rather than a random sample from all adults with epilepsy. Volunteers may differ systematically from non-volunteers in important ways such as motivation, severity of condition, access to healthcare, or willingness to try new treatments. Random assignment within the study ensures internal validity for comparing drugs L and M, but it does not address the external validity issue of who volunteered in the first place. Because the sample consists only of volunteers, results can most reasonably be generalized only to adults with epilepsy

q.s: Which statement about the power of a significance test is true?

o.l: A test performed at a significance level of α=0.01 has a higher power than the same test performed at a significance level of α=0.05.
If the probability of Type I error is decreased, the power of the test is increased.
The power of a test is equal to the probability of making a Type II error.
The power of a test is independent of the sample size.
The power of a test at a particular parameter value increases as the distance from the hypothesized value to the parameter value increases.

q.ex: Power is defined as the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, which equals 1 minus the probability of a Type II error (β). As the true parameter value moves farther from the hypothesized value under the null hypothesis, the distributions of the test statistic under the null and alternative hypotheses become more separated. This increased separation makes it easier to distinguish between the null and alternative hypotheses, reducing the overlap between their sampling distributions and thus decreasing β while increasing power. For example, if testing H₀: μ = 50, it is easier to detect μ = 60 than μ = 51 because the larger difference creates less overlap

q.s: An elevator has a posted weight limit of 4,200 pounds and an occupancy limit of 21 people. If the weights of adult males are approximately normally distributed with μ=190 pounds and σ=32 pounds, which of the following best approximates the probability that a random sample of 21 adult males will exceed the posted weight limit of the elevator?

o.l: 0.001
0.076
0.155
0.378
0.500

q.ex:
To solve this problem, we need to find the probability that the total weight of 21 adult males exceeds 4,200 pounds, which is equivalent to finding the probability that their average weight exceeds 4,200/21 = 200 pounds.

For a sample of n = 21 individuals from a normal distribution with μ = 190 and σ = 32, the sampling distribution of the sample mean has mean μ_x̄ = 190 and standard error σ_x̄ = σ/√n = 32/√21 ≈ 6.98 pounds.

Half the students from the sample were randomly assigned to a treatment group that received sleep restrictions, and the other half were assigned to a control group that received no sleep restrictions. The students were given a reading-comprehension test before the study began and at the end of two days. The mean score of the test for the treatment group was similar to that of the control group before the study. A 95 percent confidence interval constructed from the difference in mean scores (treatment minus control) at the end of two days was (−7.3,−1.5).

Based on the confidence interval, which of the following is an appropriate conclusion?

o.l: The data provide no evidence that the population of sleep-deprived students from the college has a lower mean reading-comprehension score than the population of students from the college who are not sleep deprived.

The data provide convincing statistical evidence that the population of sleep-deprived students from the college has a lower mean reading-comprehension score than the population of students from the college who are not sleep deprived.
No conclusion can be made because a confidence interval cannot be used to assess statistical evidence.
The probability that a student from the college who is sleep deprived will have a lower reading-comprehension score than a student from the college who is not sleep deprived is 0.95.
More than half the students from the college do worse on a reading-comprehension test after being sleep deprived.

q.ex: The 95 percent confidence interval for the difference in mean scores (treatment minus control) is (-7.3, -1.5). Since this entire interval lies below zero, it indicates that the treatment group (sleep-deprived students) scored lower than the control group. Because zero is not contained in the confidence interval, we can reject the null hypothesis of no difference at the 0.05 significance level. This provides convincing statistical evidence of a true difference between the populations. The negative values throughout the interval consistently support that sleep deprivation is associated with lower reading-comprehension scores. The driving route between a student’s home and the student’s high school has two traffic lights. The distribution of total time spent driving has mean 5 minutes and standard deviation 1 minute. The distribution of time spent waiting at a light has mean 0.75 minute and standard deviation 0.25 minute. The total time spent driving and the time spent waiting at a light are independent. The total travel time from the student’s home to the student’s high school consists of the total time spent driving and the time spent waiting at two lights.

What are the mean and the standard deviation of the total travel time?

o.l: The mean is 5.75 minutes and the standard deviation is about 1.03 minutes.
The mean is 5.75 minutes and the standard deviation is about 1.06 minutes.
The mean is 6.5 minutes and the standard deviation is about 1.06 minutes.
The mean is 6.5 minutes and the standard deviation is about 1.12 minutes.
The mean is 6.5 minutes and the standard deviation is about 1.5 minutes.

q.ex: The total travel time equals driving time plus waiting time at two independent traffic lights. For means of independent random variables, we add them directly: mean = 5 + 0.75 + 0.75 = 6.5 minutes. For standard deviations of independent random variables, we add the variances then take the square root. The variance of driving is 1² = 1, and the variance of each light is 0.25² = 0.0625. Total variance = 1 + 0.0625 + 0.0625 = 1.125. The standard deviation is √1.125

A six-week training program was developed to help student athletes improve performance on a certain task. To study the effectiveness of the program, researchers randomly selected 50 student athletes. The students were tested before participating in the program. Then, half the athletes were randomly assigned to participate in the program and the other half were allowed to train on their own. At the end of the six weeks, all athletes were tested again. The researchers reported that the athletes who participated in the program increased their scores, on average, by 200 points, whereas those who did not participate raised their scores, on average, by 80 points.

After reading the results of the study, Jasmine, a student athlete, decided to enroll in the program. At the end of six weeks, her score had increased by 80 points. Which of the following is an explanation for the difference between Jasmine’s score and the scores that the study reported for student athletes who participated in the program?

o.l: The results of the study were false; there must have been a bias in the sample that was not reported.
Jasmine probably did not follow the program correctly; if she had, she would have seen a 200-point increase in her score.
The increase of 200 points reported was an average; some athletes could have increased their scores by more than 200 points, and some by less than 200 points.
The sample sizes used in the study were too small for any conclusions about the training to be valid.
The study was not a well-designed experiment because causation cannot be attributed to the program.

q.ex: The study reported that athletes in the program increased their scores by an average of 200 points. An average is a measure of central tendency that represents the typical value in a distribution, but individual values naturally vary around this average. Some athletes in the program would score above 200 points of improvement, while others would score below 200 points. Jasmine's 80-point increase, though below the average, falls within the expected range of individual variation. This is a fundamental property of averages—not all individuals will match the mean value exactly. Option i3 is correct because it recognizes that the 200-point figure is an average and that individual results will vary

Which of the following statements illustrates the Law of Large Numbers?

  1. For n flips of a fair coin with one side heads, the proportion of flips that land heads up approaches 0.5 as n increases.
  2. For n tosses of a fair six-sided die with one face labeled 1, the proportion of tosses that land with the face of 1 up approaches 16 as n increases.
  3. If each of 10 consecutive tosses of a fair coin resulted in a head, the probability that the next toss of the coin will result in a tail is greater than 0.5.

o.l: I only
II only
III only
I and II only
I, II, and III

q.ex: The Law of Large Numbers states that as the number of trials increases, the sample proportion approaches the theoretical probability. Statement I correctly illustrates this: as n coin flips increases, the proportion of heads approaches the theoretical probability of 0.5. Statement II also correctly illustrates this: as n die tosses increases, the proportion of 1s approaches the theoretical probability of 1/6. Statement III is incorrect because it reflects the gambler's fallacy—the mistaken belief that past outcomes affect future independent events. The distribution of housing prices in a city includes several outliers at the upper end of the distribution and no outliers at the lower end of the distribution.

Which of the following is the most resistant, or robust, measure of center of the distribution of housing prices?

o.l: The mean, because it is affected by the outliers.
The mean, because it is not greatly affected by the outliers.
The median, because it is affected by the outliers.
The median, because it is not greatly affected by the outliers.
The mode, because the data are categorical.

q.ex: A resistant or robust measure of center is one that is not greatly influenced by outliers or extreme values in a distribution. The mean is calculated by summing all values and dividing by the count, so extreme high values (upper-end outliers) will pull the mean upward significantly. The median, however, represents the middle value when data are ordered and depends only on position, not magnitude. Even if the highest housing prices are extremely large, the median remains stable as long as the middle position doesn't change. Since the question asks for the most resistant measure in a distribution with upper-end outliers, the median is correct because it is not greatly affected by these extreme values.

The experiment has two treatment groups (face submerged vs. not submerged) and replication (25 volunteers in each group), so elements I and III are present. Instead, the 25 youngest volunteers were systematically assigned to the cold water submersion group, while the 25 oldest volunteers were assigned to the control group. This creates a confounding variable because age is now mixed with the treatment effect. Any difference in heart rate could be due to the cold water submersion, age differences, or both. Random assignment is essential to ensure treatment groups are comparable and to eliminate systematic bias.

q.ex:

The director randomly selected 5 of the groups participating in the fair and surveyed all members of the selected groups.

Which statement best describes the sampling method used by the director?

o.l: It was convenience sampling, because participants from each group were easy to contact.
It was simple random sampling, because the participants were selected at random.
It was stratified random sampling, because the director ensured that members from each group were selected.
It was cluster sampling, because the sample consisted of all members of the 5 randomly selected groups.
It was systematic random sampling, because the director selected exactly 5 groups.

q.ex: The director first randomly selected 5 groups out of 13 total groups, then surveyed all members within those 5 selected groups. This is the defining characteristic of cluster sampling: the population is divided into clusters (groups), some clusters are randomly selected, and all members within the selected clusters are surveyed. This differs from stratified sampling, where some members would be selected from every group, and from simple random sampling, where individuals would be randomly selected from the entire population without regard to group structure. The method is not convenience sampling because random selection was used, and it is not systematic sampling because that would involve selecting every nth element using a fixed interval. The correct answer is cluster

q.ex: The p-value of 0.274 represents the probability of obtaining results as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis (no difference in bitterness) were true. Common significance levels are 0.05 or 0.10, and the p-value of 0.274 exceeds both of these thresholds. When the p-value is greater than the significance level, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, meaning there is insufficient evidence to support the alternative hypothesis. The chocolatier's belief was that the new candy would be less bitter, but with p = 0.274, the data do not provide convincing statistical evidence for this claim.

Because the temperature of the water is known to have an effect, a water temperature less than 100°F will be used for the first week and a water temperature greater than 100°F will be used for the second week. Which of the following would improve this matched-pairs experiment?

Have each participant use only one of the shampoo brands, with brand randomly assigned for each participant
Have each participant use only one of the shampoo brands, with brand determined by the subject’s preference
Let each participant decide for themselves how much shampoo to use
Let each participant decide for themselves what water temperature to use, but each participant must keep the water temperature the same for both brands

q.ex: The current experimental design has a critical flaw: water temperature is confounded with time period. All participants use water below 100°F in week one and above 100°F in week two, meaning any difference in effectiveness could be due to temperature rather than shampoo brand. This eliminates the confounding variable while maintaining the matched-pairs structure where each participant serves as their own control.
